articles.title: Mechanical Thrombectomy 24 to 72 Hours after Large-Vessel Ischemic Stroke.
articles.abstract: Endovascular thrombectomy is an established treatment for acute ischemic stroke. Whether the benefit extends to patients with salvageable brain tissue in the infarct who present more than 24 hours after symptom onset or the time when they were last known to be well is uncertain. We conducted an open-label, randomized trial with blinded outcome assessment at comprehensive stroke centers in China. Patients with acute ischemic stroke from large-vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation and imaging-identified salvageable brain tissue at 24 to 72 hours were assigned to receive endovascular therapy plus standard medical care (intervention group) or standard medical care alone (control group). The primary outcome was functional status, defined by the score on the modified Rankin scale (range, 0 to 6, with higher scores indicating greater disability and a score of 6 indicating death) at 90 days, with results assessed as the distribution of scores in each group. Secondary outcomes included disability, neurologic impairment, and safety. A total of 336 patients were included in the intention-to-treat population, with 168 assigned to each group. The median time from symptom onset or from the point when the patient was last known to be well to randomization was 38.5 hours. Endovascular therapy resulted in a more favorable distribution of modified Rankin scale scores at 90 days than standard medical care alone (common odds ratio for a better functional outcome, 1.74; 95% confidence interval, 1.19 to 2.55). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 4.8% of the patients in the intervention group and in no patients in the control group, and the 90-day case fatality rate was 6.0% and 1.8%, respectively. Among patients who presented 24 to 72 hours after an acute ischemic stroke from large-vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation and had imaging-identified salvageable tissue, endovascular therapy resulted in better functional outcomes than standard care but led to a higher risk of intracranial hemorrhage and death. (Funded by the National Health Commission Capacity Building and Continuing Education Center and others; LATE-MT ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05326932.).

articles.title: Acupuncture for older adults with dementia in residential care homes: an assessor-blinded, randomised controlled trial.
articles.abstract: Dementia harms the mental health of older adults and poses a significant caregiver burden. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of acupuncture in managing cognitive decline and related symptoms in older adults with dementia. Eligible participants were recruited from 19 local residential care homes for older people in Hong Kong, China, from 5 October 2021 to 27 August 2024, in an assessor-blinded, randomised controlled trial. 118 participants were randomised to acupuncture and care-as-usual control (n=59 in each group) for 12 weeks. The analyses were on the intention-to-treat population. The primary outcome was the mean baseline-to-endpoint change of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score. Secondary outcomes included the functional independence, pain, depressive and sleep symptoms. 85.6% (101/118) of participants completed the study. The primary outcome, MoCA, was not significantly improved in week 12. Subgroup analyses showed that the treatment effect on MoCA appeared to differ across dementia severity strata. Acupuncture was superior over control in improving functional independence (the Chinese version of the Modified Barthel Index, mean difference=4.12, 95% confidence interval=0.81, 7.44, P=0.015; standardised effect size=0.29). All treatment-related adverse events were mild, and 2 nontreatment-related death cases were reported. While no significant effect in cognitive function was observed, acupuncture was associated with an improvement in functional independence, and the treatment effect on cognition might differ across dementia severity strata. This warrants further validation of the exploratory results, identifying a subpopulation of older adults with dementia who could gain more benefits from acupuncture in improving cognitive function. www.ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04305951, date of registration: 10/03/2020.

articles.title: Atacicept in IgA Nephropathy - Phase 3 Trial Final Efficacy Analysis.
articles.abstract: Atacicept resulted in a significantly greater reduction in the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo in a previously published analysis of this trial, ORIGIN 3. Final prespecified efficacy results are reported here. We randomly assigned adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy to receive weekly subcutaneous atacicept at a dose of 150 mg or placebo. We carried out final analyses of two secondary end points: the change in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at week 52 and the annualized eGFR slope through week 104; additional hierarchically tested end points and safety were assessed. Of 431 patients who underwent randomization, 428 received atacicept or placebo (214 per group). At week 52, the mean change in the eGFR was -0.11 ml per minute per 1.73 m of body-surface area (95% confidence interval [CI], -1.44 to 1.22) with atacicept and -5.69 ml per minute per 1.73 m (95% CI, -7.04 to -4.35) with placebo (mean difference, 5.58 ml per minute per 1.73 m; 95% CI, 3.68 to 7.48; P<0.001). Through week 104, the mean annualized eGFR slope was -0.60 ml per minute per 1.73 m (95% CI, -1.62 to 0.41) with atacicept and -5.60 ml per minute per 1.73 m (95% CI, -6.64 to -4.57) with placebo (difference, 5.00 ml per minute per 1.73 m per year; 95% CI, 3.55 to 6.45; P<0.001). Composite kidney-disease progression occurred in 11 patients (5.1%) in the atacicept group and in 38 patients (17.8%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.24; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.48; P<0.001); no patients in the atacicept group had progression to dialysis, transplantation, or death, as compared with 7 patients in the placebo group. Adverse events occurred in 160 of 214 patients (74.8%) in the atacicept group and in 167 of 214 patients (78.0%) in the placebo group; serious adverse events occurred in 7.0% and 15.4%, respectively. One patient (in the placebo group) died. Atacicept slowed and stabilized the decline in the eGFR as compared with placebo. (Funded by Vera Therapeutics; ORIGIN 3 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04716231.).

articles.title: The Smart MDI System in People With Type 1 Diabetes and High HBA1C: A Randomized Controlled Trial Demonstrating That Response to Alerts Drives Outcomes.
articles.abstract: The aim was to assess the efficacy and safety of the smart multiple daily injections (MDI) system versus MDI plus continuous glucose monitor (CGM) in people with Type 1 diabetes and HbA1c ≥ 8%. After a 3-week run-in, 143 participants were randomized to Smart MDI or MDI + CGM. The primary endpoint was between-group difference (Δ) in time-in-range (TIR) at 6 months, adjusted for baseline glycaemia and assessed for non-inferiority (margin 7.5%). Secondary endpoints included HbA1c (non-inferiority margin 0.4%) and superiority analyses for TIR and HbA1c. Smart MDI alerts prompt insulin bolus actions (in contrast to traditional CGM alerts), and post hoc analyses were performed to evaluate 'alert-responsiveness' on glycaemia. Alert-responsiveness findings were validated in a real-world cohort of 5507 users. Safety endpoints were assessed. At 6 months, Δ TIR between groups was 0.19 percentage points (95% confidence interval: -4.9 to 5.3), thus meeting non-inferiority; HbA1c also met non-inferiority (Δ: -0.13 percentage points, -0.46 to 0.19) but neither showed superiority. Post hoc analyses showed higher responders to alerts (those responding more than the median response rate of 28.3%, n = 31) had greater TIR gains than lower responders (n = 28) (+8.12 percentage points; p = 0.04) and HbA1c reduction (-0.6 percentage points; p = 0.02). TIR benefits in higher responders were confirmed in the real-world cohort. One episode of diabetic ketoacidosis occurred (run-in) and one severe hypoglycaemic event occurred (control arm). Smart MDI is safe and non-inferior, achieving non-inferiority to MDI + CGM regarding TIR and HbA1c. Responding to as few as 28% of alerts resulted in glycaemic improvements.

articles.title: Bleeding With Asundexian Versus Placebo in Patients With Noncardioembolic Ischemic Stroke or High-Risk TIA: OCEANIC-STROKE Randomized Trial.
articles.abstract: OCEANIC-STROKE (XXX) showed that asundexian added to antiplatelet therapy reduced ischemic stroke without significantly increasing bleeding in patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk transient ischemic attack. We characterized bleeding categories, sites, and key subgroups. In the safety population, 12 254 participants received at least 1 dose of asundexian (n=6124) or placebo (n=6130). Bleeding was categorized by International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis criteria as major, clinically relevant nonmajor (CRNM), or minor. While-on-treatment analyses included events through 2 days after the last dose, with death and permanent discontinuation as competing risks. Major bleeding occurred in 117 (1.9%) participants with asundexian and 107 (1.7%) with placebo (cause-specific hazard ratio [csHR], 1.10 [95% CI, 0.85-1.44]; =0.46). Major or CRNM bleeding occurred in 339 (5.5%) and 307 (5.0%), respectively (csHR, 1.12 [95% CI, 0.96-1.30]; =0.16), and any bleeding in 763 (12.5%) and 752 (12.3%) (csHR, 1.02 [95% CI, 0.93-1.13]; =0.65). Treatment effects for major and major or CRNM bleeding were consistent across prespecified subgroups, including planned dual antiplatelet therapy. Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 41 (0.7%) and 36 (0.6%) participants. Any gastrointestinal bleeding occurred in 186 (3.0%) and 147 (2.4%) (csHR, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.03-1.59]), and lower gastrointestinal bleeding in 102 (1.7%) and 59 (1.0%) (csHR, 1.75 [95% CI, 1.27-2.41]), primarily rectal bleeding. Any procedure-related bleeding and any mucosal bleeding did not differ significantly. Asundexian added to antiplatelet therapy reduced ischemic stroke without significantly increasing major, major or CRNM, or any bleeding. Lower gastrointestinal bleeding was more frequent with asundexian, whereas treatment effects on major and major or CRNM bleeding were consistent across prespecified subgroups. articles.title: Curcumin Suppresses Growth of Recurrent Colorectal Adenoma After Endoscopic Resection: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Multicenter Trial.
articles.abstract: Experimental and limited clinical studies suggest that curcumin has chemopreventive activity in the colorectum. This large-scale clinical trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of curcumin in patients with previously endoscopically resected colorectal neoplasia. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicenter trial enrolled patients with previously resected colorectal neoplasia. Eligible patients were randomly assigned (1:1), using a stratified, computer-generated scheme to receive oral submicron-powdered curcumin (Theracurmin; 180 mg twice daily) or identical placebo capsules for 2 years. All analyses were performed according to a modified intention-to-treat principle including all randomly assigned patients who underwent the 2-year colonoscopy. Between April 1, 2016, and March 31, 2020, 577 patients were randomly assigned to curcumin (n = 287) or placebo groups (n = 290). The detection rate of recurrent colorectal adenomas at 2 years, the primary end point, did not differ significantly between groups (risk ratio 0.98; 95% confident interval 0.82-1.16). However, the detection rate of adenomas ≥6 mm, a prespecified lesion category recommended for endoscopic resection in Japanese guidelines, was significantly lower with curcumin (risk ratio, 0.56; 95% confident interval, 0.33-0.95; P = 0.04). The per-patient number of adenomas ≥6 mm was also significantly lower ( P = 0.03), and the median size of all detected adenomas was significantly smaller in the curcumin group ( P = 0.003). The inhibitory effect seemed more pronounced in patients with higher baseline adenoma burden and in men in exploratory analyses. Treatment-related adverse events were infrequent and mild. Curcumin inhibited the growth of recurrent colorectal adenomas, despite no significant reduction in the overall incidence of recurrence. This is the first large-scale randomized clinical trial demonstrating the suppressive efficacy of curcumin against colorectal neoplasia, and also highlighting the importance of incorporating growth-related endpoints, in addition to incidence-based or detection-based end points, in chemoprevention studies (jRCTs061180079).

articles.title: Remibrutinib versus teriflunomide in relapsing multiple sclerosis (REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2): two randomised, phase 3 trials.
articles.abstract: Remibrutinib is a highly selective, potent, covalent, CNS-penetrant, oral BTK inhibitor. We assessed the efficacy and safety of remibrutinib in adult patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis. REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2 are two identical, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active comparator-controlled, parallel-group, event-driven, phase 3 trials conducted at 407 centres in 46 countries. Patients aged 18-55 years with relapsing multiple sclerosis, an Expanded Disability Status Scale score of 0-5·5, and evidence of recent disease activity were randomly assigned 1:1 to oral remibrutinib 100 mg twice daily or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily via interactive response technology. Randomisation was stratified by geographical region, MRI cohort participation, and multiple sclerosis subtype. Patients, site investigators, and trial team were masked to treatment allocation. The primary endpoint was annualised relapse rate (ARR), defined as the number of confirmed multiple sclerosis relapses per patient-year with up to 30 months of follow-up, and assessed in all randomly assigned patients. These trials are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05147220 and NCT05156281) and are ongoing, not recruiting. Between Dec 13, 2021, and Dec 30, 2025, 2632 patients were screened and 2007 patients were randomly assigned. REMODEL-1 included 1000 patients (remibrutinib 502, teriflunomide 498; mean age 38·2 years, 666 [66·6%] female, 334 [33·4%] male) and REMODEL-2 included 1007 patients (remibrutinib 504, teriflunomide 503; mean age 39·0 years, 675 [67·0%] female, 332 [33·0%] male). ARR was significantly lower with remibrutinib than with teriflunomide: 0·073 versus 0·112 (rate ratio [RR] 0·648 [95% CI 0·453-0·927]; p=0·018) in REMODEL-1 and 0·080 versus 0·116 (RR 0·688 [0·487-0·972]; p=0·034) in REMODEL-2. The most common adverse events were upper respiratory tract infection (132 [13·1%] of 1006 with remibrutinib vs 137 [13·7%] of 1001 with teriflunomide), nasopharyngitis (92 [9·1%] vs 123 [12·3%]), diarrhoea (84 [8·3%] vs 109 [10·9%]), and alopecia (58 [5·8%] vs 135 [13·5%]). Adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation were less frequent with remibrutinib (31 [3·1%]) versus teriflunomide (58 [5·8%]). The safety profile of remibrutinib was consistent with that in other indications, including no liver safety concerns. Remibrutinib was superior to teriflunomide in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis, while maintaining a favourable safety profile. These findings support remibrutinib as a potential new oral treatment option for relapsing multiple sclerosis. Novartis.

articles.title: Retatrutide Once Weekly for Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
articles.abstract: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide 1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for treating obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). In two phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials nested within larger basket trials of once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide, we assigned adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and a body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) of at least 27, without (TRIUMPH-1-OSA) or with (TRIUMPH-2-OSA) type 2 diabetes, to receive retatrutide (4, 9, or 12 mg) or placebo. The primary end point was the change in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, the average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep) at 80 weeks with 9 mg and 12 mg of retatrutide. For OSA-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy used for participants who had intercurrent events suggesting treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy used elsewhere. We also report intention-to-treat (ITT) results. A total of 243 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and 448 in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The baseline mean AHI was 58.6 and 55.9 events per hour, respectively, and the mean body weight was 119.6 and 115.9 kg. At 80 weeks, the mean changes in the AHI (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-1-OSA were -22.9 (4 mg), -34.3 (9 mg), and -31.7 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -9.9 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -13.0 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -23.0 to -3.0], -24.4 [95% CI, -34.1 to -14.7], and -21.9 [95% CI, -32.2 to -11.5], respectively). The changes with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-2-OSA were -19.2 (4 mg), -24.7 (9 mg), and -25.4 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -10.3 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -8.9 [95% CI, -15.9 to -2.0], -14.4 [95% CI, -21.6 to -7.2], and -15.1 [95% CI, -22.5 to -7.7]). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -13.2 (95% CI, -22.6 to -3.9), -24.7 (95% CI, -34.1 to -15.3), and -22.5 (95% CI, -31.9 to -13.1) in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -8.8 (95% CI, -15.8 to -1.7), -13.9 (95% CI, -21.3 to -6.6), and -15.0 (95% CI, -22.5 to -7.4) in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The mean percent change in body weight with retatrutide (key secondary end point) was -12.5 to -22.2% in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -12.1 to -18.5% in TRIUMPH-2-OSA, versus -4.8% and -5.6% with placebo (treatment-regimen estimand). The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal. In adults with OSA and obesity or overweight with or without type 2 diabetes, retatrutide resulted in significantly greater decreases in the AHI than placebo. (Funded by Eli Lilly; TRIUMPH-1 and -2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05929066 and NCT05929079.).

Medical cannabis for the treatment of insomnia.
articles.abstract: Insomnia is highly prevalent and associated with substantial individual and societal burden, while existing pharmacological treatments are limited by adverse effects and concerns about long-term use. The role of medical cannabis in the treatment of insomnia remains unclear because of limited and heterogeneous evidence. Despite increasing clinical use, current guidelines do not provide clear recommendations due to uncertainty regarding its efficacy and safety. A clear synthesis of available evidence is needed to inform patients, clinicians, and policymakers about the potential benefits and harms of medical cannabis for insomnia. To assess the benefits and harms of medical cannabis in adults with insomnia. We used CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, Global Index Medicus, and two trial registers, together with reference checking, citation searching, and contacting study authors, to identify studies for inclusion in the review. The latest search date was 5 April 2025. We included parallel randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cross-over RCTs, and cluster RCTs in adult participants with any type of insomnia comparing medical cannabis with placebo, benzodiazepine receptor agonists, benzodiazepines, melatonin receptor agonists, antidepressants, and antipsychotics. We excluded studies that were quasi-RCTs and studies using experimental and unregistered drugs, cannabis receptor antagonists and negative allosteric modulators like rimonabant, as well as modulators that enhance endocannabinoid system activity, such as fatty acid amide hydrolase inhibitors, and synthetic cannabis, like levonantradol. Our critical outcomes were quality of sleep/satisfaction with sleep, total sleep time and adverse events. Our important outcomes included sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset, daytime functioning, withdrawal symptoms, and quality of life. We used the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for parallel RCTs and the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for cross-over RCTs. We synthesized results for each outcome using meta-analysis where possible, using a random-effects model. Where this was not possible due to the nature of the data, we synthesized results narratively. We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence for our critical outcomes, daytime functioning and quality of life for the comparison of medical cannabis versus placebo. We included nine studies with 537 participants aged 18 to 76 years. Most studies included predominantly female populations (72.66%), focused mainly on participants with primary insomnia, although one study focused on insomnia associated with comorbidities. Three studies included patients with acute insomnia, and six included patients with chronic insomnia. One study compared medical cannabis with antidepressants (amitriptyline), while the other eight studies compared medical cannabis with a placebo. Two studies used licensed medications (one plant-based cannabinoid, one synthetic cannabinoid), and the other seven studies used magistral preparations. Medical cannabis versus placebo The synthesized evidence from our comparison indicates that, compared with placebo, medical cannabis may have little to no clinically meaningful effect on the quality of sleep/satisfaction with sleep (SMD -0.49, 95%CI -1.06 to 0.08, I = 91%; 7 studies, 374 participants, very low-certainty evidence), total sleep time (MD 7.68 minutes, 95% CI -23.04 to 38.39; I = 80%; 6 studies, 194 participants; very low-certainty evidence), and daytime functioning (SMD -0.34, 95% CI -0.83 to 0.16; I = 65%, 5 studies, 144 participants; very low-certainty evidence), and may improve quality of life (SMD 0.84, 95% CI -0.61 to 2.29; I = 78%; 3 studies, 95 participants; very low-certainty evidence), but the evidence is very uncertain. Additionally, medical cannabis may result in a slight increase in adverse events (OR 11.25, 95% CI 4.46 to 28.35; I = 0%; 3 studies, 98 participants; low-certainty evidence; participants with adverse events in the intervention period: 37; in the placebo period: 0; in both periods: 14; in neither period: 47). The main reasons for downgrading the certainty of the evidence were high risk of bias, serious inconsistency, and imprecision. Medical cannabis may have little to no clinically meaningful effect on quality of sleep/satisfaction with sleep, total sleep time, or daytime functioning. It may lead to an improvement in quality of life, although the evidence is very uncertain. Medical cannabis may result in a slight increase in adverse events, but the certainty of this evidence is low. Future research must address the substantial uncertainty in the current evidence by conducting adequately powered, well-designed randomized trials with longer follow-up, standardized outcomes, and detailed reporting of efficacy and safety, including long-term harms. In addition, studies should explicitly incorporate equity considerations by enrolling more diverse populations and reporting disaggregated data by sex, age, and other relevant characteristics to improve the applicability and fairness of the evidence base. This Cochrane review had no dedicated funding. Protocol: https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD016216.

The efficacy of interventions to prevent type 2 diabetes among women with recent gestational diabetes mellitus-First update of a living systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: The increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) in the decade following childbirth among women with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) warrants early intervention. A prespecified update of a systematic review and meta-analyses published in 2024 was performed, examining the efficacy of interventions to prevent T2DM among women within 5 years of a GDM-affected pregnancy. An updated search on PubMed, EMBASE and Web of Science (PROSPERO: CRD4202127989) was conducted on 14 November 2024. The primary outcome was T2DM diagnosis or measures of dysglycaemia with at least 12 months follow-up in women within 5 years of a GDM-complicated pregnancy. A Bayesian approach was adopted with results reported as effect sizes with 95% credible intervals (95% Crl), and posterior probabilities of intervention effectiveness. Nine new publications were identified in this updated search, resulting in a total of 26 publications from 25 studies (n = 7379) included. Of those, four studies involved a pharmacological intervention and 21 evaluated lifestyle interventions. There was a 15% (95% CrI: 0.69-1.04) and 32% (95% CrI: 0.40-1.07) reduction in risk and hazard ratio for T2DM, respectively, with high posterior probabilities (95.0% and 96.0%, respectively). Reductions were observed for other secondary metabolic outcomes (fasting plasma glucose, body mass index, HOMA-IR and total cholesterol). Compared to the original review, this update indicates greater certainty of the efficacy of preventive interventions for T2DM in women delivered during the first 5 years after a GDM-affected pregnancy. Evidence on the efficacy and safety of pharmacotherapy interventions is still limited.

articles.title: Development and Validation of an Adult Medical Urgency Score for US Donor Heart Allocation.
articles.abstract: One in 5 heart transplant candidates in the US die or are delisted without transplant. Donor hearts are currently allocated by a 6-status therapy-based system criticized for limited risk stratification and susceptibility to gaming. To develop a new heart allocation policy based on an objective medical urgency score that ranks candidates based on the interaction between physiology and mechanical circulatory support. Registry-based observational study using data from the US organ transplant system. All adult (aged ≥18 years) heart transplant candidates from January 2019 to August 2025 were included, split into training (2019-2023), validation (2023-2024), and test (2024-2025) datasets. A marginal structural model of 6-week mortality without transplant was estimated (the US Candidate Risk Score [US-CRS]). Eight models were compared in held-out data by weighted time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and calibration by status. Finally, US-CRS was converted into an allocation policy and a match-run simulation of waitlist reordering was performed compared with the current 6-status system. Adult heart transplant candidates were partitioned into consecutive training (n = 21 859), validation (n = 7897), and test (n = 8256) datasets (mean [SD] age, 53 [13] years; 74% male). The chosen US-CRS model included 5 laboratory values and 4 therapeutic devices (durable left ventricular assist device, intra-aortic balloon pump, microaxial flow pump, and advanced mechanical circulatory support). In test-set cross-sections of candidates actively waiting on the same calendar date, US-CRS had similar or significantly higher time-dependent AUC than the current 6-status system (mean AUC, 0.807 vs 0.693, respectively) and acceptable calibration by status, especially for candidates who received their status by exception. In match-run analysis (n = 45 530 donor hearts), a US-CRS-based system led to 67% of transplant recipients moving down in rank order and increased observed 6-week transplant-censored mortality for the first candidate on the match run from 11.2% (95% CI, 10.1%-12.5%) under the current system to 15.7% (95% CI, 13.9%-17.6%) under the US-CRS-based system. In this registry-based study of US heart transplant candidates, a US-CRS-based allocation system prioritized sicker candidates with higher mortality without transplant compared with the current medical urgency statuses.

articles.title: Dupilumab efficacy and safety in patients with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.
articles.abstract: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a complex allergic hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus species that can complicate and worsen concomitant asthma and is associated with an intense type 2 immune response in lower airways; there are no approved targeted therapies. We sought to investigate dupilumab, a fully human mAb blocking IL-4 and IL-13 via the shared IL-4 receptor alpha, in patients with asthma and ABPA. In this double-blind phase 2 trial, patients with asthma aged 12 years or older who met the clinical criteria for ABPA were randomized to dupilumab (n = 35) or placebo (n = 27) for 24 to 52 weeks; of these patients, 37.1% were receiving chronic systemic corticosteroids (SCSs). The primary end point was change from baseline in prebronchodilator FEV at 24 weeks. Additional end points included severe respiratory exacerbations and SCS use. At week 24, prebronchodilator FEV was significantly improved with dupilumab versus placebo (least squares mean change, 0.203 L vs 0.002 L; least squares mean treatment difference, 0.201 L; 95% CI, 0.08-0.33; P = .002). The adjusted annualized severe respiratory exacerbation rate per person-year was 0.695 (95% CI, 0.35-1.36) with dupilumab and 1.551 (95% CI, 0.75-3.22) with placebo, a 55.2% reduction (nominal P = .0627). At week 24, 71.4% of dupilumab recipients who required SCSs at baseline no longer required SCSs, compared with 14.3% receiving placebo. Overall safety was consistent with the known dupilumab safety profile. In patients with asthma and ABPA, dupilumab significantly improved lung function compared with placebo, reduced severe respiratory exacerbations, and was well tolerated.

articles.title: Once-Weekly Ribupatide for Weight Loss in Adults in China With Overweight or Obesity: The GEMINI-1 Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: Obesity is a major health problem in China; more pharmacotherapy choices for long-term weight management are needed. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of once-weekly subcutaneous ribupatide, a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, for weight loss in adults in China with overweight or obesity without diabetes. This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 clinical trial was conducted at 55 sites in China. From May to June 2024, adults without diabetes who had a body mass index of 28 or greater or 24 or greater with at least 1 weight-related comorbidity were enrolled, with final follow-up on June 20, 2025. Participants were randomized to receive once-weekly subcutaneous ribupatide (target doses of 2 mg, 4 mg, or 6 mg) or matching placebo for 48 weeks, with dose escalation for up to 20 weeks and concomitant lifestyle intervention. The primary outcome was change in body weight from baseline to week 48, including percent change in body weight and the percentage of participants achieving at least 5% body weight reduction, analyzed under the treatment policy estimand. Among 567 randomized participants (309 [54.5%] female; mean [SD] age was 34.4 [8.4] years, body weight was 93.0 [17.3] kg, and body mass index was 33.3 [4.5]), 514 (90.7%) completed the 48-week treatment period. Least-squares mean percentage changes in body weight at week 48 were -10.7%, -16.4%, and -17.7% with ribupatide 2, 4, and 6 mg, respectively, vs -1.4% with placebo. articles.title: ERN-RITA/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis, classification, monitoring, and treatment of childhood idiopathic (primary) angiitis of the central nervous system.
articles.abstract: Childhood central nervous system (CNS) vasculitis is a rare and serious disease for which no evidence-based consensus guidance, standardised terminology, or definitions of treatment response exist. We aimed to develop the first international recommendations for the diagnosis, classification, monitoring, and treatment of CNS vasculitis in children. Adapting the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology standardised operating procedures, an international multidisciplinary panel of 42 experts from 15 countries was assembled through the European Reference Network on Rare Immunodeficiency, Autoinflammatory, Autoimmune and Paediatric Rheumatic Diseases, and the Paediatric Rheumatology European Society. A systematic literature review across 4 databases identified 182 eligible studies, graded per the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine hierarchy. A modified Delphi survey (42 respondents) was followed by a 2-day face-to-face consensus conference (26 voting members; ≥70% agreement required). The panel formulated 83 consensus statements (3 overarching principles, 14 principles, and 66 recommendations) across 7 clinical domains. Of 182 included articles, 152 (83.5%) reported paediatric data; no level 1 evidence was identified. Key advances include an 8-domain nomenclature system replacing the 'primary/secondary' dichotomy with 'idiopathic/disease-associated' terminology, a paediatric-specific vessel wall imaging interpretive principle, a prospective risk-stratification model for disease progression, genome-wide sequencing as the preferred genetic testing approach, and formal definitions of remission, relapse, and refractory disease. None of these elements had been previously codified for childhood CNS vasculitis. These recommendations establish a comprehensive, evidence-graded framework for childhood CNS vasculitis. The absence of level 1 evidence across all domains points to the need for an international prospective registry and collaborative clinical trials.

articles.title: Drug Burden Index Stewardship to Deprescribe Anticholinergic or Sedative Drugs in Older Inpatients: A Stepped-Wedge Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: Anticholinergic and sedative medications contribute to poor clinical outcomes in older inpatients. Evidence-based deprescribing strategies are needed. This stepped-wedge cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted in 6 Australian public hospitals from January 2022 to July 2023. Participants were patients 65 years and older with Drug Burden Index (DBI; a measure of anticholinergic and sedative medication exposure) score greater than 0 at admission and hospitalized for 48 hours or more. Data were analyzed from October 2023 to May 2026. The intervention bundle had 2 components. The informational component (automated DBI score calculation displayed in the electronic medical record, deprescribing guides, patient leaflets, and education module) was present in all trial phases, although clinicians were not informed of it during the control phase. The stewardship component (study stewardship pharmacists who promoted the informational component and made patient-level deprescribing recommendations to attending teams) was delivered in the intervention phase. The informational component was promoted 1 to 2 times monthly during the sustainability phase. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients with 1 or more DBI-contributing medications deprescribed (ceased or dose reduced) at discharge compared with admission. Secondary outcomes included deprescribing recommendations in discharge summaries and in-hospital adverse events. Among 4827 included patients, 2798 (58.0%) were female, and the median (IQR) age was 83.0 (76.0-88.0) years. The proportion of patients with 1 or more DBI-contributing medications deprescribed was 38.1% (788 of 2069) in the control phase, 41.4% (326 of 788) in the intervention phase, and 37.0% (729 of 1970) in the sustainability phase. The adjusted absolute difference (aAD) between intervention and control was 5.3 percentage points (95% CI, 0.1-10.6), smaller than hypothesized. Deprescribing was predominantly by cessation; in the intervention phase, 256 of 788 patients (32.5%) had 1 or more DBI-contributing medications ceased, 91 (11.5%) had 1 or more doses reduced, and 21 (2.7%) had both. The aAD between the sustainability and intervention phase estimates was -5.3 percentage points (95% CI, -10.9 to 0.3). Deprescribing recommendations in discharge summaries were more prevalent in the intervention (176 of 751 admissions [23.4%]) than the control phase (287 of 1968 admissions [14.6%]; aAD, 10.5 percentage points; 95% CI, 6.0-15.1) and were lower in the sustainability phase (362 of 1910 [19.0%]; aAD, -4.0 percentage points; 95% CI, -8.7 to 0.8). In-hospital adverse events were similar across phases. In this stepped-wedge cluster randomized clinical trial, the intervention bundle increased deprescribing less than hypothesized, and the increase was not sustained once the stewardship component ended. articles.title: Effect of intensive blood pressure control on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes: prespecified analysis of secondary outcomes of BPROAD randomised controlled trial.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the effect of intensive compared with standard treatment of systolic blood pressure (SBP) on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes. Multicentre, open label, outcome assessor masked, randomised controlled trial. 145 clinical centres across seven geographical regions in China. 12 821 adults aged ≥50 years with type 2 diabetes, raised SBP, and increased cardiovascular risk, of whom 12 434 without probable dementia at baseline were included in this cognitive ancillary study. Further assessments were performed annually and at the end of study. Participants were randomly assigned to receive intensive treatment targeting SBP <120 mm Hg or standard treatment targeting SBP <140 mm Hg for up to five years. The primary cognitive outcome was a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment. Secondary cognitive outcomes included all cause dementia, mild cognitive impairment, changes in cognitive functions, and changes in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics. A subset of participants underwent brain MRI at baseline (n=862) and at the end of study (n=605) to assess changes in white matter lesion volume and total brain volume. 6219 participants were assigned to receive intensive treatment and 6215 to receive standard treatment. Baseline mean age was 63.7 years, and 5567 (44.8%) participants were women. After one year, mean SBP was 121.6 mm Hg in the intensive treatment group and 133.2 mm Hg in the standard treatment group. During a median follow-up of 3.8 years, the primary cognitive outcome of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment occurred in 747 participants (3.69 events per 100 person years) in the intensive treatment group and 783 participants (3.89 events per 100 person years) in the standard treatment group (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 1.06; P=0.38). In the MRI substudy (428 intensive treatment  434 standard treatment), the intensive treatment group had a smaller increase in white matter lesion volume compared with the standard treatment group (between group difference -0.09 inverse hyperbolic sine (asinh) transformed cm, 95% CI -0.15 to -0.02; P=0.01). Over a median of about four years, no statistically significant difference in incidence of a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment was observed among adults with type 2 diabetes receiving standard treatment of SBP (target <140 mm Hg) and intensive treatment (target <120 mm Hg). Intensive treatment was, however, associated with a reduction in the accrual of cerebral white matter lesion volume. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03808311.

articles.title: Regimens of vitamin D supplementation for women during pregnancy.
articles.abstract: Vitamin D deficiency is common in pregnancy and has been associated with adverse health outcomes for the mother and infant, including pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, and low birthweight. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a vitamin D intake of 200 international units (IU) per day during pregnancy. Vitamin D supplementation is recommended for women with suspected vitamin D deficiency, but it is not universally recommended. The effects of different doses (regimens) of vitamin D during pregnancy have not been established. This is an update of a Cochrane review first published in 2019, which concluded that vitamin D supplementation (at any dose) may have little or no beneficial effects on maternal or neonatal outcomes. To assess the effects of different doses of vitamin D supplementation (alone or in combination with calcium or other micronutrients) during pregnancy: more than 600 IU/day versus up to 600 IU/day, and 4000 IU/day or more versus less than 4000 IU/day. We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and relevant databases in April 2026. We included randomised trials evaluating the effects of different vitamin D regimens during pregnancy on maternal and infant health outcomes. Trials of pregnant women with pre-existing conditions or multiple pregnancies were excluded. The critical maternal outcomes were pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, and any adverse events. The critical infant outcomes were preterm birth and low birthweight. We used the Cochrane RoB 1 tool to independently assess the risk of bias in included studies. Two review authors independently assessed study eligibility and extracted data from included studies. We conducted fixed-effect meta-analyses in RevMan where it was reasonable to assume that studies were estimating the same underlying treatment effect. If substantial heterogeneity was detected, we conducted random-effects meta-analyses, using the Mantel-Haenszel method for dichotomous outcomes and inverse-variance method for continuous outcomes. We used the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of the evidence. This review update included 25 studies with 7008 pregnant women. The included studies were conducted in 14 countries between 2004 and 2024. We excluded 29 studies, identified 23 ongoing studies, and listed 21 studies as awaiting classification. The overall risk of bias of the 25 included studies was mixed. The certainty of the evidence was low for most critical outcomes due to serious risk of bias and imprecision in the results. Vitamin D at a dose of more than 600 IU/day versus up to 600 IU/day, alone or in combination with other micronutrients (19 studies, 5141 women) Vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy at doses of more than 600 IU/day, compared with up to 600 IU/day, may make little or no difference to the risk of pre-eclampsia (risk ratio (RR) 0.90, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.65 to 1.25; 8 studies, 2629 women; low-certainty evidence), gestational diabetes (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.40; 6 studies, 2373 women; low-certainty evidence), preterm birth (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.32; 7 studies, 3411 women; low-certainty evidence), or low birthweight (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.14; 6 studies, 2090 women; low-certainty evidence). Vitamin D at a dose of 4000 IU/day or more versus less than 4000 IU/day, alone or in combination with other micronutrients (14 studies, 4954 women) Vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy at doses of 4000 IU/day or more, compared with less than 4000 IU/day, may make little or no difference to the risk of pre-eclampsia (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.25; 5 studies, 2456 women; low-certainty evidence), gestational diabetes (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.35; 5 studies, 2420 women; low-certainty evidence), or preterm birth (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.19; 7 studies, 3409 women; low-certainty evidence), and probably makes little or no difference to the risk of low birthweight (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.21; 3 studies, 1637 women; moderate-certainty evidence). Adverse events in both comparisons Reporting of adverse events (e.g. hypercalcaemia, hypervitaminosis D) was heterogeneous across studies. Few adverse events were reported, and we observed no differences between groups (low-certainty to moderate-certainty evidence). Vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy at higher versus lower doses may make little or no difference to the risk of pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, or low birthweight. Future research should prioritise adequately powered trials with harmonised study designs that include more women from under-represented regions and focus on a consistently defined set of maternal and infant health outcomes. Additionally, trials should include longer follow-up to assess infant and child health outcomes beyond birth. This Cochrane review had no dedicated funding. The previous version of this review was published in 2019 (DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD013446). The original protocol for this review was registered with PROSPERO (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42018103763).

articles.title: Acute aortic syndrome rule-out criteria: development and external validation.
articles.abstract: Acute aortic syndrome (AAS) is a rare but catastrophic event, presenting with non-specific symptoms that mimic common conditions, and carries a mortality approaching 80% when missed. Current clinical tools, including the Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score (ADD-RS) and its refinement, the simplified AORTA score, achieve high sensitivity when combined with D-dimer but fail to identify a population at sufficiently low risk to safely avoid further testing. To address this gap, the Acute Aortic Syndrome Rule-Out Criteria (ARC) were developed and validated, a pragmatic bedside tool designed to safely exclude AAS in low-risk patients without additional testing. A retrospective multistep derivation and validation study was conducted. The derivation cohort included patients with confirmed AAS from the International Registry of Acute Aortic Dissection (IRAD). articles.title: Iron Repletion in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: The IRONMET-HFpEF Randomized Trial.
articles.abstract: Iron deficiency is present in >50% of patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and is associated with reduced exercise capacity and survival. articles.title: Statin-Ezetimibe Combination Therapy versus Statin Monotherapy in Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: A Prespecified Secondary Analysis of the Randomized Ez-PAVE Trial.
articles.abstract: In a target-directed low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C)-lowering strategy, the impact of the initial treatment regimen has not been investigated in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. We compared the efficacy and safety of initial statin-ezetimibe combination therapy versus statin monotherapy within intensive or conventional LDL-C-targeting strategies. In this prespecified second randomization of the randomized Ez-PAVE trial (Effects of Ezetimibe Combination Therapy for Patients With Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: Randomized Comparison of LDL Cholesterol Targeting <70 versus <55 mg/dL) conducted at 17 centers in South Korea, a total of 3048 patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease were enrolled between January 2021 and July 2022. Following the first randomization to either an intensive (<55 mg/dL) or conventional (<70 mg/dL) LDL-C-targeting strategy, patients underwent subsequent randomization (initial statin-ezetimibe combination therapy [n=1525] versus statin monotherapy [n=1523]) and were followed up for 3 years. Lipid-lowering therapy was adjusted according to a predefined protocol to achieve LDL-C targets. The primary end point was a 3-year composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, any revascularization, or hospitalization for unstable angina. The mean±SD age was 64.4±9.0 years, and 638 patients (20.9%) were female. The incidence of the primary end point did not differ between statin-ezetimibe combination therapy (128 patients [8.5%]) and statin monotherapy (119 patients [7.9%]; hazard ratio, 1.07 [95% CI, 0.83-1.37]; =0.596). Patients who received statin-ezetimibe combination therapy achieved lower median LDL-C levels during follow-up than those who received statin monotherapy in both the intensive-targeting (53 mg/dL [interquartile range, 45-62 mg/dL] versus 62 mg/dL [interquartile range, 53-74 mg/dL]) and conventional-targeting (63 mg/dL [interquartile range, 55-73 mg/dL] versus 70 mg/dL [interquartile range, 62-81 mg/dL]) strategies. During follow-up, ezetimibe was added to the treatment regimen of 241 patients (34.3%) and 177 patients (24.8%) who initially received statin monotherapy in the intensive- and conventional-targeting strategies, respectively. The treatment effect of intensive-targeting versus conventional-targeting strategies was consistent regardless of therapy regimens without significant heterogeneity (=0.583). The safety end points were similar between the groups. Within a target-directed LDL-C-lowering strategy, cardiovascular efficacy and safety did not differ significantly, whether initiated as statin-ezetimibe combination therapy or as statin monotherapy, but combination therapy facilitated achievement of a lower LDL-C target. Cost-effectiveness of recommended interventions for managing low back pain: A systematic review.
articles.abstract: Low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. Although numerous treatment approaches are recommended by international clinical guidelines, there is still limited understanding of which interventions provide the best value for money. We aimed to critically appraise and summarise the evidence on the cost-effectiveness and costs of interventions endorsed in recent guidelines to manage low back pain (LBP), compared to usual care. We searched 10 electronic databases (e.g., MEDLINE (OvidSP), EMBASE (OvidSP), PsycINFO (OvidSP)) from inception to 9th of February 2026 for cost-effectiveness studies of guideline-recommended treatments to manage non-specific LBP. The primary outcome was cost/quality-adjusted life year (QALY), which was converted to 2024 Great British Pound values, tabulated and summarised qualitatively. Secondary outcomes were direct costs (total, interventional, health service use, community services and out-of-pocket costs) and indirect costs (e.g., lost wages, lost productivity, absenteeism). We assessed methodological quality using the Consensus Health Economics Criteria (CHEC) checklist for within-trial economic evaluations or the Philips checklist for modelling studies. Our review included 20 studies (17 within-trial economic evaluations and three modelling studies), published between 2005 and 2026. Half (n = 10) focussed on chronic LBP (>3-month duration), and eight included mixed populations (i.e., acute, subacute and chronic). All studies were of non-pharmacological, non-surgical interventions, both single-modality and multimodal interventions (e.g., exercise plus spinal manipulation; diet plus physical activity). Most interventions are cost-effective at a willingness-to-pay threshold of £20,000. Moreover, interventions aiming to reduce fear and stress or support self-management in people with chronic LBP, as well as clinician-delivered interventions including yoga, acupuncture, cognitive therapy and self-management support are potentially cost-saving from the healthcare, societal and payer's perspectives, as they are both more effective and less costly than usual care (e.g., first contact management, including advice and medication). All of the evidence is derived from high-income countries, and from a considerable heterogenous body of literature. Evidence on cost-effective treatments in low- and middle-income countries remains limited. Non-pharmacological, non-surgical interventions that include education, psychological support, acupuncture and exercise seem to be cost-effective for managing LBP, compared to usual care. Improved access to and implementation of these effective treatments is urgently needed so more people can benefit from them in routine care. The review was registered on PROSPERO (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk; CRD42024510270).

articles.title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Lowering in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes.
articles.abstract: Uncertainty persists regarding the effects of intensive blood-pressure lowering in patients with type 2 diabetes. In this multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted in Brazil, patients with elevated blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and high cardiovascular risk received intensive therapy targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg or standard therapy targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary end point was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure. Of the 9476 ethnically diverse patients who were enrolled, 4745 were assigned to receive intensive therapy and 4731 to receive standard therapy. The mean (±SD) age was 64.7±8.2 years, and 5871 of the patients (62.0%) were women. The mean systolic blood pressure during follow-up (with exclusion of the first 3 months) was 121.8±10.8 mm Hg in the intensive-therapy group and 135.4±8.2 mm Hg in the standard-therapy group. During a median follow-up of 4.0 years (interquartile range, 3.9 to 4.0), a primary-outcome event occurred in 286 patients (6.0%; 1.65 events per 100 person-years) in the intensive-therapy group and in 315 patients (6.7%; 1.83 events per 100 person-years) in the standard-therapy group (hazard ratio, 0.90; 95% confidence interval, 0.77 to 1.06; P = 0.20). Serious adverse events occurred in 706 patients (14.9%) with intensive therapy and in 693 patients (14.6%) with standard therapy. Among patients with type 2 diabetes, targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg, as compared with less than 140 mm Hg, did not reduce the occurrence of major cardiovascular events. articles.title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Control in Patients with Previous Ischemic Stroke.
articles.abstract: Whether intensive blood-pressure control reduces cardiovascular risk after cerebrovascular events remains uncertain. In this multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted at 30 sites in Brazil, we assigned participants with elevated blood pressure and previous ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack to receive intensive treatment targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg or to receive standard treatment targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary outcome was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure. A total of 4368 participants were enrolled, with 2172 assigned to intensive treatment and 2196 to standard treatment. The mean (±SD) age of the participants was 63.9±11.2 years, and 2093 (47.9%) were women. During the follow-up period, excluding the first 3 months, the mean systolic blood pressure was 122.0±11.5 mm Hg (median, 119.6 mm Hg) in the intensive-treatment group and 135.2±9.7 mm Hg (median, 135.0 mm Hg) in the standard-treatment group, with a between-group mean difference of 13.1 mm Hg (95% confidence interval [CI], 12.5 to 13.8). Over a median follow-up of 3.9 years, a primary-outcome event occurred in 236 participants (10.9%; 3.25 events per 100 person-years) with intensive treatment and in 297 (13.5%; 4.11 events per 100 person-years) with standard treatment (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.67 to 0.94; P = 0.007). The composite renal outcome (sustained reduction of ≥50% in the estimated glomerular filtration rate or progression to end-stage renal disease) was more common with intensive treatment. The overall incidence of serious adverse events was similar in the two groups. Among participants with previous ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg resulted in a lower incidence of major cardiovascular events than targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. articles.title: Association Between Weight Loss on Incretin-Based Therapy and Cardiovascular Outcomes and Mortality: A Systematic Review and Meta-Regression.
articles.abstract: The primary aim was to evaluate, using aggregate-data meta-regression, whether body weight loss induced by incretin mimetic therapy is associated with reductions in three-point major adverse cardiovascular events (3P-MACE), individual cardiovascular outcomes and mortality. A secondary aim was to estimate the overall cardiovascular effects of incretin mimetics compared with placebo. A systematic review of placebo-controlled randomized trials was conducted using MEDLINE, EMBASE, CENTRAL and ClinicalTrials.gov. Eligible trials reported cardiovascular hazard ratios (HRs) and weight changes. The primary analysis was an aggregate-data meta-regression, with the prespecified moderator defined as the placebo-adjusted percentage weight difference at the latest reported follow-up time point. Standard meta-analysis was performed to estimate overall treatment effects. Sixteen randomized trials including 97 199 participants with and without diabetes were analysed. Meta-regression showed no statistically significant association between greater body weight loss and treatment HRs for 3P-MACE, cardiovascular or all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke and hospitalization for heart failure (HHF). These findings do not establish an individual-level or causal relationship. Meta-analysis showed significant reductions in 3P-MACE (15%), cardiovascular mortality (13%), all-cause mortality (12%), myocardial infarction (14%), stroke (13%) and HHF (10%). Greater trial-level placebo-adjusted body weight loss was not significantly associated with lower treatment HRs for the cardiovascular and mortality outcomes examined, including 3P-MACE and HHF. These findings do not exclude an individual-level contribution of weight loss to cardiovascular benefit or establish causality. Individual-participant-level analyses are needed to clarify the relationship between weight loss and cardiovascular outcomes.

articles.title: A Phase 2, Double-Blind, Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Study to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Acmopatide (CT-868), a Fully Biased GLP-1/GIP Receptor Agonist, in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes and Overweight or Obesity.
articles.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM)-derived glucose values versus venous plasma glucose values during oral glucose tolerance testing (OGTT) in youths with obesity, their effect on glycemic classification, and whether deconvolution-based reconstruction improves agreement. articles.title: Left Atrial Appendage Closure Versus Oral Anticoagulation in Atrial Fibrillation: An Updated Meta-Analysis of RCTs Using Reconstructed Individual Patient Data.
articles.abstract: Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a reasonable alternative to oral anticoagulation (OAC) in selected patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). We conducted an updated meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing LAAC versus OAC in patients with AF. The primary efficacy endpoint was a composite of all stroke, systemic embolism, or cardiovascular/all-cause death. The primary safety endpoint was major bleeding. Secondary endpoints included net adverse clinical events, all-cause death, nonprocedure-related bleeding, and ischemic stroke. Reconstructed individual patient data meta-analysis using a 2-stage approach and study-level meta-analysis using random-effects models were performed. Six trials enrolling 7,004 patients randomized to LAAC (n = 3,681) or OAC (n = 3,323) were included. There were no significant differences between LAAC versus OAC for the primary efficacy endpoint (difference in restricted mean survival time [∆RMST] -0.006 years, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.027 to 0.015 years, p = 0.56) or primary safety endpoint (∆RMST 0.004 years, 95% CI -0.025 to 0.034 years, p = 0.77) at 3 years. In a study-level meta-analysis, ischemic stroke was not significantly different with LAAC versus OAC (risk ratio 1.32, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.86, p = 0.09). In conclusion, the trade-off between a statistically significant lower risk of nonprocedure-related bleeding and a numerically, but not statistically, higher risk of ischemic stroke with LAAC versus OAC necessitates individualized risk assessment and shared decision-making for patients with AF at elevated risk of stroke.

articles.title: Interventions to Support Parents Whose Babies Cry Excessively: Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Parents report that around 10% to 20% of babies cry a lot without an apparent reason during early infancy. This "excessive" infant crying can lead to adverse outcomes, including parental depression, breastfeeding cessation, impaired parent-child relationships, and, in extreme cases, infant abuse. Cost-effective parent-support services are needed. To assess the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of interventions designed to support parents of excessively crying babies. MEDLINE, Embase, EconLit, Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, CINAHL and CENTRAL were searched from inception to 8th April 2025. The NIHR CRN database and handsearching were used to identify further studies. Comparative studies reporting parental outcomes for any intervention supporting parents of excessively crying infants aged ≤1 year were included. Two independent reviewers conducted data extraction and assessed risk of bias. Meta-analysis was performed when possible; otherwise, narrative synthesis was conducted. Meta-analysis found that educational interventions significantly reduced parental stress or anxiety. Narrative analyses produced mixed findings, but components common to successful educational interventions were indicated. Meta-analyses of studies administering probiotics to infants found significant improvements in parents' quality of life but not in parental depression. No safety data and limited economic evidence were found. Few studies measured similar enough parental outcomes to be pooled in meta-analysis. Risk of bias ranged from unclear to high risk. Educational and probiotic interventions show promise for supporting parents of excessively crying babies. Additional controlled trials employing evidence-based interventions and outcome measures and cost-effectiveness analyses are needed to build on these findings.

articles.title: International recommendations for the use of imaging in the diagnosis and assessment of polymyalgia rheumatica.
articles.abstract: The study aims to develop international recommendations for the use of imaging in the diagnosis and assessment of polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). An international, multidisciplinary task force of 30 members from 12 countries was convened; the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology standard operating procedures were followed. Six clinical key questions addressing the role of imaging (ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, and F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography) in diagnosis, monitoring, outcome prediction, and technical aspects in PMR were the basis for a systematic literature review. Recommendations were formulated based on evidence and expert opinion and refined iteratively until consensus was achieved. The level of agreement was assessed by voting. Three overarching principles and 7 recommendations were developed. PMR remains primarily a clinical diagnosis. Imaging is neither required to confirm PMR in patients with a high clinical probability of the disease nor to exclude PMR in case of low clinical probability. Imaging is most useful in patients with intermediate pretest probability (ie, atypical presentations or suspected alternative/overlapping conditions). No single imaging modality demonstrated sufficient accuracy to be recommended as a first-line test; therefore, imaging should be individualised according to clinical presentation, differential diagnoses, access, and local expertise. Vascular imaging should be performed when overlap with giant cell arteritis is suspected, whereas systematic screening for subclinical vasculitis is not supported by current evidence. Utilising imaging for disease monitoring or outcome prediction is currently not recommended. These recommendations provide the first evidence-based guidance for the use of imaging in PMR, reinforcing clinical assessment as the cornerstone of diagnosis and positioning imaging as a context-driven adjunct.

articles.title: Effects of Exercise Type and Duration on Pain, Function, and Quality of Life in Patients With Knee Osteoarthritis: A Systematic Review With Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: To compare the effects of aerobic exercise, resistance exercise, and combined interventions on pain, function, and quality of life (QoL) in patients with knee osteoarthritis (OA) at the short term (≤12 weeks) and long term (>12 weeks).  Intervention systematic review with Bayesian network meta-analysis (NMA).  MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE, CENTRAL, CINAHL, PEDro, AMED, and SPORTDiscus were searched from inception until July 2025.  We included randomized controlled trials of patients with knee OA that evaluated exercise interventions aimed at improving pain, function, and QoL.  Using random-effects models, the NMA synthesized effect sizes and ranked interventions by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA), with evidence certainty assessed via the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework.  Thirty-five trials (n = 3808 patients) were included. For pain, short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effect among the interventions (standardized mean difference [SMD] = -0.937, low certainty). For function, short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effect estimates (SMD = -0.590, low certainty), followed by long-term aerobic exercise (SMD = -0.540, very low certainty). Short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effect (SMD = 0.663, low certainty) for improving QoL.  Aerobic and resistance exercise, alone or in combination, and delivered over the short- or long-term, improved pain, function, and QoL for patients with knee OA. Short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had clinically meaningful improvements for pain, with relatively favorable effects on function and QoL. Evidence regarding the clinical significance of long-term exercise interventions was limited. .

articles.title: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Pure Aortic Regurgitation: The Randomized SEASON-AR Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: For patients with severe pure aortic regurgitation (AR) at high surgical risk, guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) is often the only available option. Transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is an established treatment for aortic stenosis and has also been evaluated in patients with pure AR. However, no adequately powered randomized trial has compared TAVR with GDMT alone in this population. We conducted a prospective, investigator-initiated, multicenter, randomized, open-label trial in China. Patients with severe pure AR for whom surgery was considered difficult or unacceptable by the local heart team or who persistently declined surgery were randomly assigned at a 1:1 ratio to receive transfemoral TAVR with the VitaFlow system plus GDMT or GDMT alone. The primary end point was a composite of all-cause death, disabling stroke, or heart failure rehospitalization at 1 year. We assigned 210 patients with severe pure AR to the TAVR group (n=109) or GDMT group (n=101) at 18 centers. At 1-year follow-up, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the primary end point was significantly lower in the TAVR group than in the GDMT group (8.3% vs 24.8%; hazard ration [HR], 0.31 [95% CI, 0.14-0.66]; =0.001), driven primarily by a reduction in heart failure rehospitalization (3.7% vs 21.3%; HR, 0.16 [95% CI, 0.06-0.47];  < 0.001). TAVR was associated with higher rates of major or life-threatening bleeding and new permanent pacemaker implantation, most of which occurred within 30 days after the procedure. Among patients with severe pure AR, TAVR plus GDMT significantly reduced the rate of all-cause death, disabling stroke, or heart failure rehospitalization at 1 year compared with GDMT alone despite higher 30-day rates of major or life-threatening bleeding and new permanent pacemaker implantation. articles.title: Home Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation With Gamified Cognitive Control Training for Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has emerged as a home-based treatment in major depressive disorder (MDD), although its effects are typically small to moderate and inconsistently observed. Because tDCS may act synergistically with behavioral interventions, combining both approaches represents a promising strategy for developing more effective home-based treatments for MDD. To investigate the feasibility, safety, and efficacy of home-based tDCS and concurrent gamified cognitive control training (CCT) in adults with MDD. This multicenter, double-masked, parallel-group, randomized clinical trial with follow-up at week 10, masking checks at 2 time points, and expectancy assessments was conducted at 3 university hospitals in Latvia, Germany, and Israel between June 22, 2021, and August 8, 2024. Participants included adults aged 18 to 65 years with MDD, 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores of at least 13, and no or stable antidepressant medication. Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to active tDCS (2 mA; anode F3, cathode F4) plus a gamified CCT or sham tDCS plus a sham game. Participants were asked to complete 30 home treatment sessions (30 minutes each) over 6 weeks with software-assisted electrode positioning. The primary outcome was feasibility, defined as completing at least 20 of 30 sessions with greater than 50% probability. The secondary outcome was efficacy, measured as change in Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) scores from baseline to week 6. Of 111 enrolled participants, 109 were included in the modified intention-to-treat sample (55 in the active group and 54 in the control group; mean [SD] age, 33.1 [10.6] years; 69 female [63.3%]). Feasibility criteria were met, with 86 participants (78.9%) completing at least 20 sessions (lower bound of 1-sided 95% CI, 71.5%). The MADRS scores improved significantly in both groups at week 6, indicating insufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis of no difference in the mean change in MADRS score from baseline to 6 weeks between the 2 treatment groups (difference, 0.89 [95% CI, -1.37 to 3.15]; P = .44; Cohen d, 0.10 [95% CI, -0.15 to 0.34]). Results were similar at follow-up (week 10). Adverse events were balanced between groups. This RCT of home-based tDCS combined with CCT in adults with MDD was feasible and safe but did not demonstrate superior efficacy over the control condition. Future studies should refine the mechanistic alignment between stimulation and cognitive interventions to optimize treatment effects. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04953208.

articles.title: Performance of 0/1 h versus 0/3 h pathways in patients with suspected myocardial infarction: a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
articles.abstract: In patients with suspected myocardial infarction, the 0/1 h pathway (blood draws at 0 h and 1 h) is recommended in current guidelines for early risk stratification. However, individual trials used different safety outcomes, and efficacy outcomes were inconclusive or not assessed. We conducted a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis of all randomised controlled trials to synthesise the totality of the evidence, assess heterogeneity across trials, and evaluate clinically relevant outcomes using harmonised definitions across trials. In this systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis, we searched PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Scopus, and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform from inception to July 6, 2026, without language restrictions, for randomised trials comparing the safety and efficacy of 0/1 h versus 0/3 h pathways (blood draws at 0 h and 3 h, ie, standard care). Individual participant data were obtained and outcome definitions were harmonised. The primary analysis used a two-stage random-effects meta-analysis. After receipt of the individual participant data but before data harmonisation or analysis, the primary safety outcome was refined to a composite of all-cause death or new type 1 myocardial infarction within 30 days, from the originally specified composite of all-cause death or any new myocardial infarction. The primary efficacy outcomes were emergency department length of stay and direct discharge from the emergency department. This meta-analysis is registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261383452). Our systematic review identified five randomised trials, all of which provided individual participant data. Among these, the definition of the primary safety outcome varied, and in four trials emergency department length of stay was not reported for the whole analysis population. We included 110 933 patient presentations (55 489 managed with the 0/1 h pathway and 55 444 managed with the 0/3 h pathway). Within 30 days, all-cause death or new type 1 myocardial infarction occurred in 446 patient presentations (0·8%) with the 0/1 h pathway versus 562 patient presentations (1·0%) with the 0/3 h pathway (random-effects pooled odds ratio [OR] 0·83 [95% CI 0·45-1·53]; I=62·9%; τ=0·143). Emergency department length of stay was 314 min (IQR 211-481) in the 0/1 h pathway group versus 308 min (209-453) in the 0/3 h pathway group (random-effects pooled geometric mean ratio 1·03 [95% CI 0·85-1·25]; I=99·2%; τ=0·024). Direct discharge from the emergency department occurred in 37 190 patient presentations (67·0%) with the 0/1 h pathway versus 36 485 patient presentations (65·8%) with the 0/3 h pathway (random-effects pooled OR 1·31 [95% CI 0·79-2·16]; I=97·8%; τ=0·156). Across the available randomised trials, short-term adverse event rates were low with both pathways, but the pooled safety estimate remained imprecise. On average, earlier cardiac troponin retesting did not reduce emergency department length of stay or clearly increase direct discharge, and substantial between-study heterogeneity indicates that treatment effects might not translate uniformly across health-care systems. For hospitals considering transitioning from a 0/3 h to a 0/1 h pathway, implementation decisions should take broader diagnostic and organisational considerations into account. articles.title: Near-infrared Autofluorescence Probe Versus Visual Identification for Parathyroid Detection and Functional Preservation During Total Thyroidectomy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: To assess whether PTeye-guided identification increases the number of parathyroid glands (PGs) preserved in situ and reduces hypoparathyroidism compared with visual identification alone. Injury or inadvertent removal of PGs during thyroidectomy is the main cause of postoperative hypoparathyroidism. Reliance on visual inspection makes intraoperative PG identification difficult. Probe-based near-infrared autofluorescence (NIRAF) systems such as PTeye provide real-time, tissue-specific feedback that may enhance PG detection and preservation. In this single-center, prospective, randomized trial, patients undergoing first-time total thyroidectomy were allocated to PTeye-assisted or visual PG identification. Procedures were performed by 2 senior and 3 junior surgeons. The primary outcome was the number of PGs identified. Secondary outcomes included inadvertent parathyroidectomy, autotransplantation, and transient and last follow-up hypoparathyroidism. Among 154 randomized patients (77 per group; mean age 53.4±14.3 y; 84.4% female), PTeye increased the mean number of PGs identified (3.81 vs. 2.73; P <0.001) and the proportion with 3-4 PGs preserved in situ (98.7% vs. 87.0%; P =0.004). Inadvertent parathyroidectomy was less frequent with PTeye (5.2% vs. 20.8%; P =0.004). Junior surgeons performed more autotransplantations than senior surgeons when using PTeye (33.3% vs. 10.5%; P =0.015). Female sex ( P =0.047), ≤2 PGs preserved ( P =0.008), and autotransplantation ( P =0.010) predicted low postoperative day-1 parathormone serum level. articles.title: Ianalumab for the Treatment of Patients with Sjogren's Disease.
articles.abstract: Sjögren's disease is a complex, systemic autoimmune disease with no approved targeted therapies. articles.title: Imaging for diagnosis, monitoring and outcome prediction in polymyalgia rheumatica: a systematic literature review and meta-analysis informing an international task force.
articles.abstract: To summarise evidence on imaging for the diagnosis, monitoring and outcome prediction in polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) to inform an international task force. Six research questions across diagnostic, monitoring, prognostic and technical aspects were defined. A systematic literature review searched Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, Epistemonikos and the Cochrane Library (through July 2025), including prospective and retrospective cohort studies (≥20 patients) as well as case–control and cross-sectional studies for diagnostic aspects. Test performance was summarised descriptively and meta-analysed using bivariate random-effects models when ≥2 low or some concerns on risk-of-bias (RoB) studies were available. Forty-nine studies were included: 32 on diagnosis, 6 on monitoring, 13 on outcome prediction and 8 on technical aspects (some studies covered ≥1 aspect). No study was graded as low RoB. Diagnostic studies identified useful imaging lesions (eg, extracapsular and bilateral inflammatory patterns of shoulders and hips), but few were validated in independent cohorts. Diagnostic accuracy of positron emission tomography scores was reduced in the case of prior treatment and when used to differentiate PMR from other inflammatory diseases. Glucocorticoids substantially reduced sensitivity across modalities, highlighting the value of timely imaging when indicated. Data on monitoring and outcome prediction were sparse and heterogeneous. This systematic literature review serves as a basis for the formulation of international recommendations on the use of imaging in PMR. Available evidence was heterogeneous and of limited quality but revealed distinct imaging lesions and scores that can support PMR diagnosis. Well-designed prospective studies and external validations are needed.
